HEADLINE: Stan strong in streaming wars
TEXT:
Stan chief executive Mike Sneesby says an alignment with CBS’s Showtime, local productions and unwavering support from the joint-venture partners are key for the company’s ongoing success as competition ramps up in Australia’s video streaming market.

In an investor presentation last week, Stan, which is 50-50 owned by Nine Entertainment and Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review, revealed it had 600,000 active subscribers or households, 1.4 million sign-ups and an estimated 1.5 million active users.

Mr Sneesby said after 18 months the pay entertainment market has three clearly defined segments: traditional premium pay TV, mid-tier skinny bundle packages and pure-play subscription video on-demand, where Stan sits.

Competition is tough in SVOD with smaller local players closing shop and the first major casualty, Presto, a joint venture between Seven West Media and Foxtel, falling earlier this month.

The Financial Review revealed Amazon was mulling over a launch of its video streaming service, Prime Video, next month to be headlined by The Grand Tour, starring former Top Gear hosts Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May.

‘‘Our deal with Showtime is much more than securing a long-term content supply out of Showtime ... both Showtime and HBO could have been direct to consumer players in our market,’’ Mr Sneesby said.

HBO has signed a long-term agreement with Foxtel and Showtime.

Netflix is targeting 50 per cent of its content to be original productions – the streaming giant is expected to spend more than $US5 billion on programming this year.

‘‘Amazon and Netflix are increasingly production houses and studios themselves, the net result of that means they are spending less money acquiring content and competing more as a studio,’’ Mr Sneesby said.

‘‘The Hollywood studios are really supportive of independent local leaders like us.’’ Last week, Stan launched the second series of its original production No Activity and has several other new shows in development.

The company said its conversion rate from free trials to paid subscribers was 73 per cent to 75 per cent and churn has dropped significantly over the last 18 months. Stan expects to cash break-even in the second half of the 2018 financial year.

‘‘Our sign-up run rate is accelerating ... churn is falling, interest in our brand is increasing ... converting into cheaper and cheaper cost per acquisition. Every one of those metrics drives our business plan,’’ Mr Sneesby said.

Stan is able to take advantage of the reach of its shareholders Nine and Fairfax through the combined assets of free-to-air television as well as print and digital news.

HEADLINE: Light not always light: Oztam
TEXT:
The chief executive of Australian television audience measurement company Oztam says sought-after ‘‘light TV’’ viewers change their consumption habits and cannot be measured over a single week or device.

Television broadcasters are competing directly for attention and advertising dollars with digital giants such as Facebook, Twitter and Google.

Increased broadband speeds and the rise of online streaming services and digital alternatives have given rise to what the media industry has dubbed ‘‘light TV’’ viewers, who are watching less TV and filling their time online.

Light viewers watch less than 1.5 hours of television a day, medium viewers watch 1.5 to 3.5 hours a day and heavy viewers watch more than 3.5 hours a day.

Light TV viewers are highly sought after by advertisers for being younger, more educated and residing within higher income households.

However, OzTAM chief executive Doug Peiffer told The Australian Financial Review that light TV viewers were not consistent and, over the period of a month, most Australians watched television, but the range of devices used was increasing.

Research by OzTAM indicated, over a month, viewers considered light could become medium or heavy users in different weeks. Over a four-week period, 29 per cent of light viewers were light every week.

Overall, light viewers watched television on 40 per cent of days. On 24 per cent of days they were light viewers, 12 per cent of days they were medium viewers and 4 per cent of days they were heavy users, according to OzTAM.

‘‘The screen activity of light viewers in particular fluctuates: they may spend relatively less time with their TV one week while filling in their viewing with second screens,’’ Mr Peiffer said.

‘‘The following week they may be in front of their TV sets more.

‘‘This is why isolating a single week in a light viewer’s life is a flawed approach.

‘‘Advertisers can reach light viewers effectively by spreading a TV campaign across more channels and screens over several weeks. Over any four-week period, TV reaches 85-90 per cent of Australians in all age groups: including light, medium and heavy viewers.’’ Factoring in other devices for video consumption also had an impact. Light viewers had access to 8.8 screens, either TV, smartphone, tablet or, PC versus 6.5 for heavy viewers.

Australia’s TV broadcasters, free-to air and subscription, have moved to capture those audiences that are consuming video across a range of devices, with their own live-streaming and catch-up services. Freeview is planning the launch of a mobile app that will include all the free-to-air network’s streaming services.

Earlier this year, the FTA and pay TV industry in Australia formed marketing body Think TV. The Nine, Seven, Ten and Foxtel bosses will even come together next month for a chief executive discussion panel at Rethink TV.

Seven West Media chief executive Tim Worner said television was multiplatform.

‘‘Your mobile phone is a TV set, and 15 per cent of TV viewing is on laptops, tablets, smartphones, anywhere there is a screen,’’ Mr Worner said.

‘‘We’ve had more change in our industry in the past two years than in the previous 20 but some things don’t change. One of those is that you simply cannot beat TV for return on investment.

TV makes advertisers more money than any other media. Period.’’ Nine Entertainment chief executive Hugh Marks said TV was brand safe and provided scale audiences.

‘‘And rather than scoring our own homework based on assumptions, guesses or, in some cases, just inaccurate claims, the measurement of TV audiences is reliable, transparent, established and, most importantly, world class,’’ Mr Marks said.

HEADLINE: Instagram chief connecting the globe
TEXT:
Marne Levine has worked for the Clinton and Obama administrations, Harvard University, a start-up, Facebook and now Instagram.

But the Ohio native has never had a grand plan to lead her to exactly this point.

‘‘I’ve been really fortunate ... I have this way of thinking about it ... which is I’ve meandered with a sense of purpose,’’ Ms Levine, who is now chief operating officer at social media, photo-sharing business Instagram, told The Australian Financial Review in Sydney on a recent trip.

‘‘I’ve been in each place for some period of time, but I haven’t necessarily been that person who has had it all planned out from the beginning.’’ Ms Levine refers to a famous quote by Apple founder Steve Jobswhentalking about her storied resume: ‘‘You can’t connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backwards. So you have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future.’’ Ms Levine’s resume includes the US Department of Treasury in the Clinton Administration, chief of staff for the Harvard president, director of product management for Revolution Money and National Economic Council chief of staff and special assistant to the president for economic policy during the first Obama administration.

She took the COO role at Instagram in 2015 after four years as Facebook vice-president for global public policy.

Facebook bought Instagram for $US1 billion in 2012.

Acommontheme across all the roles the Harvard Business School graduate has had is being mission-driven.

‘‘I went into politics and government because you’re really mission-driven in terms of using government to help improve the lives of as many people as possible,’’ she said. ‘‘What attracted me to Facebook and Instagram was the same thing, the mission of connecting the world.

‘‘The power of images transcends borders, generations, cultures and languages and it really brings people together.’’ Images and increasingly video are allowing greater insights into the lives of celebrities, politicians, sports stars and everyday people.

‘‘I think that people are interested in ideas and concepts. People are also interested in knowing whothathuman being is,’’ MsLevine said.

‘‘There’s a lot of dimensions to every human being – what they’re like with their family, what they like to eat, what they like to do in their spare time, who they interact with. You can see that through photo. You can really see that through video.’’ MsLevine is focusingongrowing the Instagram platform for consumers and advertisers. Last year Instagram opened up advertising to all marketers, following contained trials, andnowhas 500,000 advertisers worldwide.

In June the platform used Australia as the launch country for its new advertising business tools. Ms Levine said Australia’s strong small business community and rapid take-up of technology made it a natural fit for launch.

‘‘The vast majority of the advertisers wehave are small businesses,’’ she said.

Instagram now as more than 7 million active users in Australia and 500 million globally, with 80 per cent of those being outside the United States.

‘‘The really important thing is relevance ... understanding who you’re trying to target, understanding what someone’s interests are and putting the right story in front of the right person at the right time.’’

HEADLINE: Selling Australia to world not as easy as it sounds
TEXT:
Selling Australia to the rest of the world can, paradoxically, be one of the easiest and most difficult briefs in the country.

On one hand, beautiful beaches, landscapes, food, wildlife and people ...

not the hardest of sells.

On the other hand, with taxpayer money funding Tourism Australia and a population that will scrutinise every detail of how they and their country are marketed to the world, the spotlight is definitely bright.

Last month, IPG Media brands’ UM Australia was confirmed as Tourism Australia’s new media buyer, joining creative agency Clemenger BBDO as the tourism body’s agency partners.

Tourism Australia chief executive John O’Sullivan told The Australian Financial Review the change will bring an increased focus on targeted marketing.

‘‘For organisations like us it’s becoming a real challenge around how do we effectively target those end consumers and particularly in the context that we’re taxpayer funded, we have to be very, very efficient in the way we do that,’’ he said.

‘‘We produce amazing content, we have some of the most amazing content in the world to play with, but if we’re serving you up with content that’s not relevant to your travel plans ... you’re just going to switch us off.’’ Tourism Australia wants to know the interests of consumers, not just their location, to present offers with contextual relevance. ‘‘You’ve got such emotive content; how can we get it tailored to the right person and then offer it to the right person, with the right partnerships, with the right intent, so it comes from a ‘sometime’ quality to ‘I’m actually going to go two months from now’ ... capitalising on inspiration and bringing the purchase is something that we can do now because of smartphones,’’ UM chief executive Ross Raeburn said.

Tourism Australia chief marketing officer Lisa Ronson said the focus on digital enables the body to shift money to campaigns that are working from those that aren’t.

‘‘For our category, being travel, being aspirational, it’s freezing cold in the UK on a Monday morning and Christmas is over, you’re thinking ‘Oh, I need a holiday’ ... it’s those sorts of moments where if we serve up a warm Australian video to them, that’s going to be a lot more engaging because it’s in that right moment, in that right mindset,’’ Ms Ronson said.

Tourism Australia presents some unique challenges. There are subtle nuances that need to be considered when marketing around the world. For example, some campaign material can have over 100 different edits. Some cultures may not allow drinking alcohol, so a food and wine campaign needs to be made without wine.

Clemenger BBDO Sydney managing director Emily Perrett said working with TA allows it to take new approaches into areas such as 360-degree video to try to make Australia a desirable destination.

‘‘It gives us more options ... because of how extensive [TA’s] knowledge of the traveller is, you can be super creative but in a way that you know is safe and works,’’ she said.

HEADLINE: Bishop warns on Trump
TEXT:
Foreign Minister Julie Bishop has warned a Donald Trump presidency may pose a threat to the Asia-Pacific, suggesting the controversial Republican candidate would have to be persuaded to maintain a US presence in the region.

In her most forthright commentary yet on the US election, Ms Bishop appeared to back Hillary Clinton, whose campaign has been rattled anew by a fresh probe into emails she kept on a private server.

"US engagement in our region is important for us," Ms Bishop told the ABC. "I believe that will continue under Hillary Clinton.

"It will be up to our region, including Australia, to persuade a Trump administration to focus on the Asia-Pacific," she said.

Ms Bishop talked up Mrs Clinton's regional credentials, describing her as the architect of Barack Obama's famous pivot towards the Asia-Pacific region.

"She sees the US as having a global leadership role," said Ms Bishop.

"Candidate Donald Trump does not.

"He sees the US as having got a raw deal from globalisation and he would focus more on domestic matters," she warned.

Her comments came as the US Federal Bureau of Investigation's shock decision to scrutinise previously undetected emails linked to its lapsed investigation into Mrs Clinton threw the election into upheaval and cast doubt on a presumed comfortable Democratic win.

An angry Mrs Clinton shifted to damage control at the weekend, attacking FBI director James Comey for his "deeply troubling" move just 11 days before the election to probe emails reportedly found on the laptop of the estranged husband of the candidate's close adviser.

The emboldened and hyperbolic Republican presidential nominee, Donald Trump, likened the twist to the 1970s Watergate scandal.

The FBI's Mr Comey wrote to a Republican-led congressional committee on Friday to advise that his agency would review newly discovered emails in an unrelated case to see if the material contained classified information.

The emails, he said, "appeared to be pertinent" to the past investigation into whether Mrs Clinton and her aides mishandled classified materials when she exclusively used a private email account and server for government work as secretary of state between 2009 and 2013.

The FBI "cannot yet assess whether or not this material may be significant", Mr Comey wrote. It quickly emerged through US media that thousands of emails were uncovered on the seized laptop of disgraced former Democratic politician, Anthony Weiner.

Independent veteran pollster John Zogby said the FBI's renewed activity was "like a punch to the gut" for Mrs Clinton's White House aspirations.

"Just as some undecided voters were on the verge of concluding that perhaps she is the lesser of two evils, they may just change their minds," he said.

"It reminds people of why they have not liked her."

The revelation on Friday rattled investors on Wall Street betting on the stability of a Clinton victory on November 8.

The news triggered a sudden 0.8 per cent drop in the US S&P 500 from its intraday high, before some of the losses were recouped. The Mexican peso, a proxy for a Clinton victory due to opponent Donald Trump's anti-Mexico policies, fell nearly 2 per cent at one stage.

Markets were earlier buoyed by data showing the US economy grew at its fastest pace in two years, an annual clip of 2.9 per cent in the September quarter.

Almost 20 million Americans - about 15 per cent of the estimated total voters - have voted early. About 5 per cent of voters are estimated to be undecided on the two candidates.

The controversy may help Republicans maintain control of the Senate by motivating conservative voters.

Mrs Clinton, who has been fending off a range of controversies, is not trusted by about two-thirds of American voters.

As well as the lingering fallout from her decision to break US State Department protocol and use a personal email server at her home for diplomatic communications, she has been forced to fend off claims of conflicts of interest connected to her family's charity, the Clinton Foundation.

WikiLeaks has warned in the lead-up to the election it will continue to release damaging emails stolen from Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta.

Ms Bishop on Sunday agreed "any political candidate would see [the latest FBI probe] as a hurdle coming so late in the campaign".

Director of the International Security Program at the Lowy Institute Dr Euan Graham agreed Ms Bishop's comments were her strongest yet and suggested Australia was concerned about a Trump victory.

"It speaks to some wider concern within the government. [They] could be a reaction to the events of the last few days of the FBI re-opening it's inquiry and some hearts might be fluttering as to whether there's still an outside shot the election is not a foregone conclusion," Dr Graham said.

He said the government could also be calling on the US to continue to focus on the Asian region. "There may be a sense there's a flag that's been raised to look after the Asian alliances," he said.

Ms Bishop's concerns coincide with difficulties in Australia's relationship with China, which blew up after the foreign minister called on the country to adhere to the ruling of an international court against its nine-dash line in the South China Sea. There was also ill-feeling after bids for S.Kidman & Co and Ausgrid from Chinese companies were rejected by Treasurer Scott Morrison.

Adding to the complications in the region, the US and Australia have been unsettled by Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte's declaration in China that he had "separated" from the US.

On Sunday Ms Bishop effectively broke her silence on Mr Duterte's trip to China, suggesting he should be more grateful for the US.

"There will be concerns if he does seek to distance the Philippines from the United States because the United States has been the principal security guarantor for our region and many nations, including the Philippines and Australia have benefited enormously from the US presence. I hope President Duterte is appreciative of the fact that we have all benefited from the US presence in the region," she said.

HEADLINE: Fundie's $53m dividend cheque
TEXT:
Fund manager Peter Cooper has defied market trends to record a bumper profit and pay a $60 million dividend, $53.4 million of which would have gone directly to him, documents lodged with the corporate regulator reveal.

Melbourne-based Cooper Investors, which manages more than $10 billion for clients that include large superannuation funds, charities and wealthy families, made a net profit of $59 million in the 2016 financial year.

The result was up from a $52 million net profit the previous year, while management and performance fees rose to $118 million compared to just less than $90 million in 2015.

A member of the BRW Rich List, Mr Cooper will have received the vast majority of the $60 million dividend, given he owns 89 per cent of the firm he founded in 2001. The total dividend was up from $28 million in 2015.

As the chief investment officer at Cooper Investors, Mr Cooper oversees five funds, including the top-performing CI Brunswick Fund, which delivered a 12.46 per cent return for the year to June 30 against its benchmark S&P ASX 200 Accumulation Index, which was up only 0.56 per cent in the same time.

The Brunswick fund, named for the inner-city Melbourne suburb in which Mr Cooper grew up, has outperformed its benchmark by almost 10 per cent since inception in July 2004. About 22 per cent of its funds are held in stalwarts such as Brambles and Wesfarmers, while its other shareholdings include turnaround stories such as Sims Metals and cyclical stocks like Boral.

While about 90 per cent of Mr Cooper's holdings are in Australian equities, the firm has opened the CI Asian Tiger Fund and the CI Global Equities funds in recent years.

Meanwhile, Sydney firm Vinva Investment Management recorded a net profit of $35 million for the 2016 financial year, its accounts show. That result for Vinva, which manages about $18 billion, was down slightly from $37 million in 2015.

Vinva paid its shareholders, which include portfolio manager and principal Nicholas Burt, total dividends of $36 million last November, its financial accounts show. It has yet to declare a 2016 dividend.

Melbourne's Evans and Partners, which in September announced a deal to merge with Dixon Advisory to create a firm with 8000 clients with $20 billion under management, recorded a 13 per cent fall in net profit in 2016 to $8.2 million. Revenue was up 8 per cent to $73.4 million.

The company's annual report said three business units - private wealth, institutional and equity capital markets - recorded revenue rises, but the corporate advisory division was hindered by a downturn in equity capital markets in the second half of the financial year.

David Evans founded the stockbroking and advisory firm in 2007 and is the company's executive chairman. The Dixon Advisory merger is expected to be finalised by the end of November.
